paragraphs: A person should not think that the more he sleeps, the more benefit it is to the body — for all the eminent physicians agreed that a person should not sleep less than six hours at night, nor more than eight hours, for excessive sleep will harm him. It follows that this is agreed upon by all physicians: sleeping more than eight hours harms the body, and one who sleeps six hours has thereby fulfilled his obligation regarding his body's health. Therefore a Jewish man, who is also obligated to look after the health of his holy soul, should not sleep more than six hours, since he fulfills his bodily-health obligation with that much, and the remaining hours of the night he should devote to the health of his soul through the study of Torah. However, if on some night he happens to sleep less than this measure of six hours — which suffices for his bodily health — and adds to the hours devoted to the health of his soul, he can be confident that no harm or deficiency will come to him with regard to his bodily health. Therefore, on the night of Friday, the night before Rosh Chodesh, and likewise the nights of the month of Elul and the Ten Days of Repentance and the like, if a person sleeps less than the measure of six hours, his heart can be confident and at ease that nothing will be lacking to his bodily health because of this.

And although the entire night is a time for sleep, nevertheless it is better that the sleep take place in the first half of the night and not in the second half, and there is benefit in this both from the physical side, for the health of the body, and from the spiritual side, for the rectification of the soul and the rectification of the worlds. And one eminent physician wrote that from the seventh hour of the night until noon resembles the days of ascent, and from noon until evening resembles the days of standing, and from evening until the end of the sixth hour of the night resembles the days of descent. Therefore one who stays awake at the beginning of the night, which is the first half, and sleeps in the second half, resembles one who is occupied during the days of descent and rests during the days of ascent. And in the book Ruach Chaim, page 90, it is written in the name of a certain renowned sage that going to sleep early in the evening and rising early in the morning bring a person health, wisdom, and strength. Also, women who are constantly occupied with work for some hours of the night — it is good that they accustom themselves to sleep at the beginning of the night and rise in the night watch for their work, as it is written, "She rises while it is yet night, and gives food to her household" (Proverbs 31:15).

clarification.explanation: One should not think that the more a person sleeps, the better it is for the body — the eminent physicians agreed that one should not sleep less than six hours a night, nor more than eight, since excessive sleep harms the body. Therefore one who sleeps six hours has already fulfilled his obligation regarding his body's health, and the remaining hours of the night he should devote to the health of his soul through the study of Torah. If on some night he sleeps less than six hours (in order to add to his Torah study), there is no need to worry about physical harm — for example, on Friday night, the night before Rosh Chodesh, and the nights of the month of Elul and the Ten Days of Repentance. Although the entire night is a time for sleep, it is preferable to sleep in the first half of the night and be awake in the second half — both for reasons of physical health and for spiritual reasons (the rectification of the soul and of the worlds). One eminent physician described it thus: the seventh hour of the night until noon resembles days of [spiritual] ascent, noon until evening resembles days of standing, and from evening until the end of the sixth hour of the night resembles days of descent. Therefore one who is awake at the beginning of the night (the first half, the "days of descent") and sleeps in the second half (the "days of ascent") loses the better opportunity. Women who work at night should also accustom themselves to sleep at the beginning of the night and rise in the night watch for their work (as it is written, "She rises while it is yet night, and gives food to her household").
takeaways: Physicians say six to eight hours, but a Jewish man should not sleep more than six — devoting the rest of the night's hours to Torah study; and one should sleep mainly in the first half of the night and be awake in the second half, for reasons of both health and spirituality.

paragraphs: One who rises at midnight and studied Torah, but was not able to continue studying until morning light because he was forced to sleep — nevertheless, he should make an effort to rise from his sleep a bit before dawn to engage in Torah, in order to join the night with the day through the study of Torah, as is explicit in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, in Sha'ar HaKavanot, that a person must be awake at midnight and recite Tikkun Chatzot and engage in Torah; and if he cannot remain awake for the entire second half of the night, so be it — he may go back to sleep, provided that he gets up again about half an hour before dawn to engage in Torah. And this is [the meaning of] what is written, "I will awaken the dawn" (Psalms 57:9) — I am the one who awakens the dawn — for the main point is that one be awake at the time of dawn. And one must be careful about this joining of night and day also in the evening, at the end of the day, joining the day with the night through the study of Torah.

clarification.explanation: One who rises at midnight to study Torah, but cannot remain awake until morning and is forced to go back to sleep, should nevertheless make an effort to get up again a little before dawn in order to engage in Torah, so as to join the end of the night with the beginning of the day through study. As the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote: one must rise at midnight, recite "Tikkun Chatzot," and engage in Torah; if he cannot stay awake through the entire second half of the night, he may go back to sleep, provided he gets up again about half an hour before dawn to engage in Torah. This is the meaning of the verse "I will awaken the dawn" — I am the one who awakens the dawn — meaning that the main point is to be awake at the time of dawn. This joining of night and day is also important in the reverse direction — in the evening, joining the day with the night through the study of Torah.
takeaways: One who cannot remain awake through the entire second half of the night should go back to sleep, but must be careful to rise again about half an hour before dawn, so as to join the night with the day through the study of Torah.

paragraphs: One who fears Heaven should be diligent and rewarded by hastening to relieve himself before dawn, in such a way that he does not "join" night and day while he is in the privy. And he must pay close attention to this matter and be careful about it. And one who stays awake the whole night, having performed Tikkun Karet, or [on] the night of Shavuot and Hoshana Rabbah, about which we wrote that he should recite the morning blessings after midnight — only the blessing over the Torah should he recite after dawn. And if he is in doubt about the rising of dawn, not knowing whether it has risen or not, he should be careful, during those moments when he is in doubt, to recite piyyutim, songs, and praises, and not sit in silence.

clarification.explanation: One who fears Heaven must be careful to relieve himself before dawn, so that he does not "join" night and day precisely while he is in the privy (which is not a fitting place for that sacred moment of transition). One must pay special attention and be careful about this. One who stays awake the whole night (such as on the night of Tikkun Karet, the night of Shavuot, or the night of Hoshana Rabbah mentioned earlier) recites the morning blessings after midnight, but recites the blessing over the Torah only after dawn. If he is in doubt as to whether dawn has risen or not, he should use the time of doubt to recite piyyutim, songs, and praises, and not sit in silence.
takeaways: One should hasten to relieve himself before dawn, so as not to be in the privy at the exact moment of transition from night to day.
One who stays awake the whole night recites the morning blessings after midnight, but the blessing over the Torah only after dawn; during a time of doubt, he should recite piyyutim and praises.

paragraphs: The time for Tikkun Chatzot agreed upon according to the true Kabbalah is twelve hours after the midpoint of the day, when the sun is directly over a person's head, for that is certainly the midpoint of the day, as our teacher the Rashash, of blessed memory, wrote in Nehar Shalom. Now, it is known what the Rav Beit David, of blessed memory, wrote in siman 36, that the "sunrise" (hanetz hachamah) our Sages spoke of in several matters concerning the mitzvah of Keriat Shema and prayer is not when the sunrise becomes visible to us on the earth, but rather one hour before the sun rises over the earth and becomes visible to us — and he brought proofs for this; see there. Now, in earlier times, in our town of Baghdad, the custom regarding the taking of the lulav was not to recite the blessing until the sun rose and became visible to us. And the same law applies regarding Keriat Shema and prayer. But from the year [given by an abbreviation in the source], the custom regarding the lulav changed, following the reasoning of Beit David, of blessed memory, due to the pressure of the congregation, and from this the custom spread also to Keriat Shema and prayer, to act according to the reasoning of Rav Beit David, of blessed memory. Nevertheless, with all this, regarding Tikkun Chatzot, we do not follow [the calculation] as its sunrise becomes visible to us on the earth. And one who is scrupulous with himself to be awake at the exact point of midnight should also be careful according to the reasoning of Beit David, of blessed memory; and likewise one who is scrupulous about the time after midnight — it suffices for us to follow the reasoning of Beit David, of blessed memory. And I have heard that the Chasidim in the Holy City of Jerusalem, may it be rebuilt and reestablished, also do not follow the reasoning of Beit David regarding Tikkun Chatzot, but rather calculate from the actual visible sunrise on the earth.

clarification.explanation: The time of "Tikkun Chatzot" agreed upon according to the true Kabbalah is exactly twelve hours after the true midpoint of the day (when the sun is directly overhead) — so wrote the Rashash. There is an opinion (Beit David) that the "sunrise" the Sages spoke of regarding Keriat Shema and prayer is not the sunrise visible to the eye, but one hour before it. In Baghdad, the custom used to be, regarding the taking of the lulav, to recite the blessing only when the sun was actually visible, and not according to this earlier calculation; but from a certain year they began to follow the lulav custom according to the opinion of "Beit David" due to communal pressure, and from this the custom spread also to Keriat Shema and prayer. Nevertheless, regarding Tikkun Chatzot, one does not follow this earlier calculation — it should be calculated from the sunrise actually visible. Both one who is scrupulous to be awake at the exact point of midnight, and one who is scrupulous to recite Tikkun Chatzot immediately after midnight (not earlier), may follow the calculation of "Beit David"; and I have heard that the Chasidim of Jerusalem also calculate Tikkun Chatzot from the time of the sunrise visible to the eye, not according to the earlier calculation.
takeaways: The time of Tikkun Chatzot is determined by exactly twelve hours from the true midpoint of the day (sun overhead), and not according to the earlier calculations of "Beit David" that are followed in other halachot, such as the lulav.

paragraphs: Tikkun Rachel is not recited during the days of the Omer, nor during the Ten Days of Repentance on weekdays. And it is the custom of the Chasidim in the Holy City, may it be rebuilt and reestablished, that Tikkun Chatzot is not recited after the molad, before Rosh Chodesh, even though confession (viduy) is recited on that day — and so we have done as the custom here in our town, may it be protected. And it is written in Kaf HaChaim, ot 35, that Tikkun Rachel is not recited in a house of mourning nor in the house of a groom; see there. And in my responsum in my holy books, Rav Pe'alim, I gave, with the help of Heaven, reasons for this according to the hidden wisdom, and I concluded that even an individual by himself should not recite Tikkun Rachel in the house of a groom. However, on the night of a brit milah, the individual may recite it privately and in a whisper, but the father of the boy himself should not recite it, since it is his festive day.

clarification.explanation: "Tikkun Rachel" (the part of Tikkun Chatzot dealing with mourning over the destruction) is not recited during the days of the Omer, nor during the Ten Days of Repentance on weekdays. It is the custom of the Chasidim of Jerusalem not to recite Tikkun Chatzot (the Rachel portion) after the molad and before Rosh Chodesh, even though confession is recited on that very day — and the same was done in Baghdad. It is also said that Tikkun Rachel is not recited in a house of mourning nor in the house of a groom. Rabbi Yosef Chaim adds, in his responsum, mystical reasons for this, and rules that even an individual, by himself, should not recite Tikkun Rachel in the house of a groom; but on the night of a brit milah, an individual may recite it privately and in a whisper — except for the father of the boy himself, who should not recite it, since it is his day of celebration.
takeaways: Tikkun Rachel is not recited during the days of the Omer, the Ten Days of Repentance (weekdays), from the molad until Rosh Chodesh, or in a house of mourning or of a groom; the exception: on the night of a brit milah, an individual (not the father of the boy) may recite it privately.

paragraphs: Women do not recite Tikkun Chatzot, and in my holy book, Rav Pe'alim, I wrote, with the help of Heaven, correct reasons why women should not recite Tikkun Chatzot, and also should not recite the Tanakh [reading] on the night of the festival of Shavuot. And the custom of the women in our household is that they do not recite Tikkun Chatzot, nor do they recite the study for the night of the festival of Shavuot, but the study of Mishneh Torah and Tehillim on the night of Hoshana Rabbah is their custom to study. And I asked our beloved friend, the great and pious sage, our teacher Rabbi Eliyahu, about the custom of women in the Holy City, may it be rebuilt and reestablished, regarding Tikkun Chatzot, and he answered: we have not seen nor heard of a woman reciting Tikkun Chatzot.

clarification.explanation: Women do not recite Tikkun Chatzot. Rabbi Yosef Chaim wrote in his responsum the reasons for this, and also ruled that women do not recite the Tanakh study of the night of Shavuot. The custom of the women in his household was not to recite Tikkun Chatzot nor the study of the night of Shavuot, but they did study Mishneh Torah and Tehillim on the night of Hoshana Rabbah. Rabbi Yosef Chaim asked a sage in Jerusalem about the custom of women there regarding Tikkun Chatzot, and received the answer that they had never seen nor heard of a woman reciting Tikkun Chatzot.
takeaways: Women do not recite Tikkun Chatzot and do not study the special reading for the night of Shavuot, but they do take part in the study of Mishneh Torah and Tehillim on the night of Hoshana Rabbah.

paragraphs: Tikkun Leah is not recited on the night of Shabbat, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot, and Shemini Atzeret, and likewise it is not recited on Chol HaMoed of Pesach; but on Chol HaMoed of Sukkot, Tikkun Leah is recited.

clarification.explanation: "Tikkun Leah" (the second part of Tikkun Chatzot, dealing with hope and consolation) is not recited on the nights of Shabbat, Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Pesach, Shavuot, Sukkot, Shemini Atzeret, and also not on Chol HaMoed of Pesach. But on Chol HaMoed of Sukkot, Tikkun Leah is recited.
takeaways: Tikkun Leah is not recited on the nights of Shabbat and the festivals, nor on Chol HaMoed of Pesach, but it is recited on Chol HaMoed of Sukkot.

paragraphs: Once dawn has risen, one should not recite Tikkun Chatzot, neither Tikkun Rachel nor Tikkun Leah, as they wrote in the name of Rabbi Moshe Zacuto, of blessed memory. And as for what is written in Lev Chaim, part 1, siman 6, that even after dawn, as long as the time for tzitzit and tefillin has not arrived, one may still recite Tikkun Chatzot — one should not rely on this, for these matters were given to be recited only according to the Kabbalah, and from the implication of the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, it appears that this tikkun exists only while it is still night.

clarification.explanation: From the moment dawn has risen, one should no longer recite Tikkun Chatzot at all — neither Tikkun Rachel nor Tikkun Leah — as they wrote in the name of Rabbi Moshe Zacuto. There is an opinion (Lev Chaim) holding that even after dawn, as long as the time for tzitzit and tefillin has not yet arrived, one may still recite Tikkun Chatzot — but Rabbi Yosef Chaim rules that one should not rely on this, since the recitation of Tikkun Chatzot was given only according to the Kabbalah, and it is implied from the words of the Ari, of blessed memory, that the tikkun exists only while it is still night.
takeaways: From the moment dawn rises, Tikkun Chatzot should not be recited at all, neither Tikkun Rachel nor Tikkun Leah, contrary to the lenient opinion of "Lev Chaim."

paragraphs: If there is not enough time before dawn to recite both Tikkun Chatzot and to engage in Torah study, Tikkun Chatzot takes precedence; and likewise in the month of Elul, when Selichot are recited, the recitation of Tikkun Chatzot precedes the Selichot.

clarification.explanation: If there is not enough time before dawn both to recite Tikkun Chatzot and to engage in additional Torah study, it is preferable to recite Tikkun Chatzot. The same applies in the month of Elul, when Selichot are recited — the recitation of Tikkun Chatzot takes precedence over the recitation of Selichot.
takeaways: When time is limited, Tikkun Chatzot takes precedence over additional Torah study and over the recitation of Selichot in the month of Elul.

paragraphs: At the time one recites Tikkun Chatzot, he should change his place from the beginning of Tikkun Rachel until after he finishes Tikkun Leah, whether he recites it in his home or in the synagogue; and before he recites the Petichat Eliyahu Zachur LaTov, he then sits in his principal place where he wishes to study. However, at a time when only Tikkun Leah is recited, and not Tikkun Rachel, there is no need to change his place at all. And those who are accustomed to place ash on the spot where the head-tefillin rest, when reciting Tikkun Rachel, as our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, wrote — their custom is to leave it there until the completion of Tikkun Leah, and so it stands to reason.

clarification.explanation: At the time of reciting Tikkun Chatzot, one should change his place of sitting from the beginning of Tikkun Rachel until after the completion of Tikkun Leah — whether he recites it at home or in the synagogue. Only before reciting "Petichat Eliyahu Zachur LaTov" (which comes at the end of Tikkun Leah) does he return to sit in his principal place where he studies. But at times when only Tikkun Leah is recited (and not Tikkun Rachel), there is no need to change one's place at all. Those accustomed to place ash on the spot of the head-tefillin during the recitation of Tikkun Rachel (following the custom of the Ari) leave it there until the completion of Tikkun Leah.
takeaways: During Tikkun Rachel and Tikkun Leah one should change his sitting place (generally to a plain, humble spot), and return to his usual place only just before Petichat Eliyahu Zachur LaTov.

paragraphs: This is the order of reciting Tikkun Chatzot according to the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory:

Sit at the beginning of Tikkun Rachel near the doorway, close to the mezuzah, and it is good that the door of the room in which you are reciting be open, if there is no cold there. And before you recite Tikkun Rachel, spread a kerchief or another light garment on the ground, the size of your seat, for one should not sit directly on the bare ground. And remove your shoes and sit there barefoot, and cover your head with a cloak or another garment, and take ash from a fire and place it on the spot where the head-tefillin rest, and bow your head and press your face against the ground itself, and intend by this to grieve over the burning of the Torah that became ash, and also intend to grieve that because of our many sins, since the Temple was destroyed, the secrets of the Torah and its mysteries were handed over to the external forces — which is called the exile of the Torah, because of our many sins.

And then you shall begin to recite "By the Rivers of Babylon" (Psalms chapter 137), and intend to weep in this psalm over the destruction of the Temple. And afterward, "A Psalm of Asaph" (Psalms chapter 79), and intend to weep in this over the killing of the righteous. And afterward, "Remember, O Lord, what has befallen us" (Lamentations chapter 5) until the end, and you shall repeat the verse "Restore us." And afterward the verses "Look, etc.," "You, etc.," "Why, etc.," "To the afflicted, etc." (Isaiah 63:15-18), "And now, etc.," "Do not be angry beyond measure, etc.," "Your holy cities, etc.," "Will You hold back for these, etc." (Isaiah 64:7-11), and do not recite verses beyond this. And afterward the verses of consolation: "Upon your walls, etc.," "And give Him no rest, etc.," "The Lord has sworn, etc.," "For those who gather it, etc.," "You will arise and have mercy on Zion, etc.," "For Your servants have taken pleasure, etc." (Psalms 102:14-15), "He builds Jerusalem, etc." (Psalms 147:2) — and thus Tikkun Rachel is completed.

clarification.explanation: Rabbi Yosef Chaim describes the precise order of Tikkun Chatzot according to the Ari: one sits at the beginning of Tikkun Rachel near the doorway, close to the mezuzah, with the door open (if there is no cold). Before reciting, one spreads a kerchief or light garment on the floor (one should not sit directly on the bare ground), removes one's shoes and sits barefoot, covers the head with a cloak or garment, takes ash and places it on the spot where the head-tefillin rest, bows the head and presses the face against the ground itself — with the intention of grieving over the burning of the Torah that became ash, and over the fact that because of our sins the secrets of the Torah were handed over to the forces of impurity (the "exile of the Torah"). Then one begins reciting chapters of Tehillim ("By the Rivers of Babylon" over the destruction of the Temple, "A Psalm of Asaph" over the killing of the righteous, passages from Lamentations, and consolation verses arranged from Isaiah and Tehillim) — all with the intention of weeping over the destruction, concluding with verses of consolation about the building of Jerusalem. With this, "Tikkun Rachel" is completed.
takeaways: Tikkun Rachel is recited sitting on the floor barefoot, with the head covered and ash on the spot of the tefillin, with the intention of grieving over the destruction of the Temple and the exile of the Torah, and concludes with verses of consolation.

paragraphs: And afterward you shall begin Tikkun Leah. And you shall say "As the deer" [Psalm], and the Psalm "Judge me" (Psalms chapters 42-43), and the Psalm "May He answer you" (Psalms chapter 20), and the Psalm "The earth is the Lord's" (Psalms chapter 24), and the Psalm "May He be gracious to us and bless us" (Psalms chapter 67), and the Psalm "I will thank the Lord with all my heart" (Psalms chapter 111), and the Psalm "When Nathan the prophet came to him" (Psalms chapter 51) — and you shall recite this psalm aloud, with weeping, supplication, and entreaty, seeking forgiveness from before Him, blessed be He, for your sins. And afterward you shall say, "How long shall there be weeping in Zion and mourning in Jerusalem; arise and have mercy on Zion and build the walls of Jerusalem," and you shall intend Zion as corresponding to Rachel and Jerusalem as corresponding to Leah. And afterward you shall sit in your principal place and engage in Torah study.

And there are those accustomed to say, after the aforementioned Tikkun Leah, the Psalm "When the Lord returns the captivity of Zion" (Psalms chapter 126), and the supplication "Merciful King, have mercy upon us, etc." and "May it be Your will, etc." And although these are not mentioned in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, there is no concern in reciting them, since reciting them at the end of Tikkun Leah as arranged by our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, presents no problem, and so we are accustomed to recite them. However, there are places where, after Tikkun Rachel, they recite the text "Woe is me over the exile of the Shechinah, etc.," as is written in the prayer books, and this matter is not mentioned in the words of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory; and although from reasoning it appears there is no concern in reciting it, nevertheless we have not been accustomed to recite it. And I inquired about the custom of the Chasidim in the Holy City, may it be rebuilt and reestablished speedily in our days, and they answered me that it is not their custom to recite the aforementioned "Woe is me," but their custom is to recite, after the completion of Tikkun Leah, "Merciful King, etc." and the Psalm "When [the Lord] returns, etc.," in order to conclude with consolation. And they recite Kaddish Yehei Shelama.

I also asked our beloved friend, the great and pious sage, our teacher Rabbi Eliyahu Mani, may the Merciful One preserve and redeem him, about the custom of the Chasidim in the Holy City, may it be rebuilt and reestablished speedily in our days, whether they recite the Psalm "When Nathan the prophet came to him" (Psalms chapter 51), and the verse "How long shall there be weeping in Zion," even on days when confession (viduy) is not recited, and he answered that the plain custom is to recite the Psalm "When [Nathan] came to him" even at a time when confession is not recited. And he further wrote: In the Sabbatical year in the Land of Israel, may it be rebuilt and reestablished speedily in our days, when Tikkun Rachel is not recited, in my humble opinion the verse "How long shall there be weeping in Zion" should also not be recited, since Rachel is alluded to in this verse, and so it should not be recited on all the days when Tikkun Rachel is not recited. And I have heard that in the congregation of Chasidim in Beit El, may it be established in righteousness, they also do not recite it. And afterward I saw in Minchat Aharon, klal 6, siman 3, that on a day when Tachanun is not recited, one should not recite this verse; and in my humble opinion it does not depend on Tachanun, but rather depends on the recitation of Tikkun Rachel — thus far his words, may the Merciful One preserve and redeem him.

And after the psalms of Tikkun Leah, the custom is to recite Petichat Eliyahu Zachur LaTov, because it is necessary to attach the study of Torah for its own sake (Torah lishmah) to Tikkun Leah, for there lies the secret of Torah lishmah, which corresponds to the letter Heh, as is known. And I found it written that after Petichat Eliyahu Zachur LaTov, one should recite the teaching of Rabbi Shimon bar Yochai written in the holy Zohar, Parashat Noach, page 65, and Pekudei, page 265: "Rabbi Shimon said: I raised my hands in prayer on high, that when the supernal will is above, etc. ... until: fortunate is the portion of the righteous in this world and in the world to come" — and as I shall write further below in Parashat Miketz, see there.

And know, that it is written in Sha'ar HaMitzvot of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, regarding the prohibition of pronouncing the Name as it is written, that even if one reads it out in the following spelled-out form — Yod Heh Vav Heh — one should be careful, in the aforementioned Petichat Eliyahu, to say it thus: "Within it is the letter Yod, and the letter Heh, and the letter Vav, and the letter Heh" — for since he says the word "letter" with each of them, this is not considered pronouncing the Name. And likewise he should be careful, when saying afterward "Rabbi Shimon arose, etc.," to say: "And this is the letter Yod and the letter Heh and the letter Vav; but the letter Heh is the Shechinah, which is not counted in the sum of 39, rather the letter Yod and the letter Heh and the letter Vav, which together add up to 39, etc." And he shall do likewise regarding other wordings in the holy Zohar and the Tikkunim.

clarification.explanation: After Tikkun Rachel one begins "Tikkun Leah" — reciting a number of Psalms ("As the deer pants," "Judge me," "May He answer you," "The earth is the Lord's," "May He be gracious to us and bless us," "I will thank the Lord with all my heart," and "When Nathan the prophet came to him" — Psalm 51, recited with weeping and entreaty and a request for forgiveness for one's sins). Afterward one says "How long shall there be weeping in Zion... arise and have mercy on Zion" (where "Zion" alludes to Rachel and "Jerusalem" to Leah), and then returns to one's usual seat to continue Torah study. Some are accustomed to add the Psalm "When the Lord returns the captivity of Zion" and the supplication "Merciful King" — even though these are not mentioned in the words of the Ari, there is no concern in reciting them. In some places, after Tikkun Rachel, they recite the text "Woe is me over the exile of the Shechinah," but the custom of Rabbi Yosef Chaim and the custom of the Chasidim of Jerusalem is not to recite this. There is a difference between communities regarding the recitation of Psalm 51 and the verse "How long shall there be weeping in Zion" on days when confession is not recited, and in the Sabbatical year in the Land of Israel, when Tikkun Rachel is not recited, the verse alluding to Rachel should also not be recited. After Tikkun Leah one recites "Petichat Eliyahu Zachur LaTov," since it is necessary to attach the study of "Torah for its own sake" to Tikkun Leah (which alludes to the secret of Torah lishmah). There is also a precise instruction in the name of the Ari as to how to pronounce the Name's letters during the recitation of Petichat Eliyahu: one should say "within it is the letter Yod and the letter Heh and the letter Vav and the letter Heh" — inserting the word "letter" before each letter takes it out of the category of pronouncing the Name as it is written; and likewise in "Rabbi Shimon arose," one should say "and this is the letter Yod and the letter Heh and the letter Vav."
takeaways: Tikkun Leah consists of Psalms and concludes with Petichat Eliyahu Zachur LaTov, which symbolizes the transition to the study of Torah for its own sake; there are differences in custom between communities regarding additions and the recitation of certain verses at certain times.

In Petichat Eliyahu one should say "the letter Yod and the letter Heh and the letter Vav and the letter Heh" — inserting the word "letter" before each letter takes it out of the category of pronouncing the Name as it is written.

paragraphs: It is the custom of our town, may it be protected, to recite the Psalm "By the Rivers of Babylon," and the verses of Lamentations, "Remember, O Lord, what has befallen us," and the verses of Isaiah, all in a mournful melody (kinah) that awakens weeping and breaks the heart, and they are not recited with their [regular cantillation] trope. And I inquired about the custom of the Chasidim in the Holy City, may it be rebuilt and reestablished speedily in our days, and they answered that their custom is to recite the aforementioned verses in a mournful melody, and not with their [regular] trope.

clarification.explanation: It is the custom in Baghdad to recite the Psalm "By the Rivers of Babylon," the verses of Lamentations ("Remember, O Lord, what has befallen us"), and the verses of Isaiah — all in a mournful melody (kinah) that awakens weeping and breaks the heart, and not with the ordinary cantillation. The Chasidim of Jerusalem were likewise accustomed to recite these verses in a mournful melody and not with the ordinary cantillation.
takeaways: The verses of Tikkun Rachel (By the Rivers of Babylon, Lamentations, Isaiah) are recited in a mournful melody that awakens weeping, not with the ordinary cantillation.

paragraphs: In many places it is customary to recite confession (viduy) before reciting Tikkun Chatzot, and this is likewise the custom of our town; therefore, in the month of Elul and the Ten Days of Repentance, when Selichot are recited and confession is recited within the Selichot, one should not recite the confession [again] before Tikkun Chatzot.

clarification.explanation: In many places, and likewise in Baghdad, it is customary to recite confession before reciting Tikkun Chatzot. Therefore, in the month of Elul and the Ten Days of Repentance, when Selichot — which include confession — are recited, one should not recite the confession again before Tikkun Chatzot (since it has already been recited within the Selichot).
takeaways: The confession ordinarily recited before Tikkun Chatzot is not recited again during Elul and the Ten Days of Repentance, since it is already included in the recitation of the Selichot.

paragraphs: It is the custom of the Chasidim in the Holy City of Jerusalem to recite Kaddish Yehei Shelama after Tikkun Leah, because they recite the Kaddish after the [portion of] Scripture; but the custom of our town is to recite Petichat Eliyahu Zachur LaTov after the Scripture, and then they recite Kaddish al Yisrael, and there is no strictness about this — each should follow his own custom.

clarification.explanation: It is the custom of the Chasidim of Jerusalem to recite "Kaddish Yehei Shelama" after Tikkun Leah, because they recite the Kaddish after the reading of Scripture ("mikra"). But the custom of Baghdad is to recite "Petichat Eliyahu Zachur LaTov" after the Scripture, and only then to recite Kaddish al Yisrael. There is no strictness in this matter — each community should follow its own custom.
takeaways: There is no essential difference between the customs regarding where the Kaddish is placed at the end of Tikkun Chatzot — each community continues according to its own custom.

paragraphs: What King David, peace be upon him, wrote, "I have set the Lord before me always" (Psalms 16:8) — this is a great principle in the Torah, that a person should never let his mind wander from the fear of the Lord, blessed be He, and the splendor of His majesty, and should always keep in mind that His glory, blessed be He, fills the whole earth. Therefore he is obligated to conduct himself in ways of modesty even in a room by himself with the door closed, so that he should not stand completely naked, except when necessary, such as in the bathhouse and the like. But when changing his clothes, he should not remove his trousers until he has put on the undergarment [shirt], or he should change his trousers while the old undergarment is still on him, and afterward change the undergarment — and this manner, of putting on the trousers first, is more correct. And he should not say, "Who sees me naked?" — rather he should remember that the glory of the Lord, blessed be He, fills the whole earth, and be careful out of respect for the Lord, blessed be He.

clarification.explanation: The verse "I have set the Lord before me always" expresses a great principle of the Torah: a person should never let his mind wander from the fear of the Lord and the honor of His majesty, but should always remember that the glory of the Lord fills the whole earth. From this stems the obligation to behave modestly even alone in a closed room — not to stand completely naked except when necessary (such as in the bathhouse). When changing clothes, one should not remove one's trousers before putting on the upper garment; rather, one should change the trousers while the old upper garment is still on, and only then change the upper garment — and this is the correct order (putting on the trousers first). One should not think "who sees me naked" — rather remember that the Lord's glory fills the whole earth, and be careful on that account, for the honor of the Lord.
takeaways: One must behave modestly even alone in a closed room, out of awareness of the constant presence of the Lord; when changing clothes, one should be careful never to be left completely naked — changing the trousers while still wearing the old upper garment, and only then changing the upper garment.

paragraphs: One should be careful not to wear two garments interwoven one inside the other together, for this is prone to cause forgetfulness. He should also be exacting about his undergarment (chaluk), to wear it in its proper way; and if he put on his undergarment inside out, he should remove it and put it on properly. He should not walk with an overly upright posture, nor should he walk with his head uncovered, and he should be careful not to sit with his head uncovered even for a moment, except when necessary. And even in the outer room of the bathhouse he should cover his head until he enters the inner room, and it is forbidden to mention the [Divine] Name with the head uncovered; and a covering [made] by his own hand does not suffice — only a covering by the hand of another person suffices.

clarification.explanation: One must be careful not to wear two garments interwoven one inside the other (tangled together), since this is likely to cause forgetfulness or confusion. One should be exacting to wear the undergarment (chaluk) properly; if it was put on inside out, one should remove it and put it on correctly. One should not walk with an overly upright posture (out of arrogance), and should not walk or sit with the head uncovered even for a moment, except when truly necessary. In the bathhouse (in the outer room) one should cover the head until entering the inner room. It is forbidden to mention the Name with the head uncovered; covering the head with one's own hand does not suffice for this — only if another person's hand covers it does it help.
takeaways: One should not walk or sit with the head uncovered (except when necessary), and certainly should not mention the Name of the Lord with the head uncovered; covering with one's own hand does not suffice — only with the hand of another person.

paragraphs: When one washes his hands, he should wash the right hand first; and when he washes his entire body, he should wash his head first; and when he dresses, he should put on [the covering for] his head first — though it suffices with the small, thin cap that one wears on the head beneath the larger hat or turban. And people who have no undercap but only the one red cap called "fez" should put it on before the undergarment [shirt].

clarification.explanation: When washing the hands, one should wash the right hand first. When washing the whole body, one should wash the head first. When dressing, one should put on the head-covering first — though it suffices to put on first the small, thin cap worn under the larger hat or turban. One who has no undercap, only a single cap (such as the red "fez"), should put it on before the shirt/undergarment.
takeaways: In the order of washing and dressing, the "head" takes precedence — one washes the right hand first, washes the head first in bathing, and puts on the head-covering (even the small one) before the rest of the clothing.

paragraphs: One should not walk barefoot, for our Sages, of blessed memory, said: a person should always sell whatever he has and buy shoes for his feet, for one who withholds shoes from his feet is like one placed under a ban [by Heaven]. And he should be careful not to walk without socks, called in Arabic "jorab" (stockings), whether in summer or in winter, and especially at the time of prayer, of which it is said, "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel" (Amos 4:12).

clarification.explanation: One should not walk barefoot — as our Sages said: a person should sell the beams of his house in order to buy shoes for his feet, for one who denies himself shoes is considered "excommunicated" [banned by Heaven]. One must be careful not to walk without socks ("jorab") in either summer or winter, and especially at the time of prayer, as it is said, "Prepare to meet your God, O Israel."
takeaways: One is obligated to wear shoes and socks (not go barefoot) in every season, especially in preparation for prayer, as an expression of respect and readiness to stand before the Lord.
